Faulkner County by the numbers

Where is Faulkner County and how did it form?

Faulkner County is in central Arkansas, with Conway as both county seat and largest city. It was created on April 12, 1873, from parts of Conway and Pulaski counties, and is named for Sandford C. "Sandy" Faulkner, the planter and fiddler linked to the Arkansas Traveler tale.

The county covers about 664 square miles, where the Ozarks meet the Arkansas River Valley. It borders Cleburne, White, Lonoke, Pulaski, Perry, Conway and Van Buren counties. Interstate 40 helped turn Conway and nearby towns into commuter communities for Little Rock.

County seatConway
Area664 square miles
2020 Census population123,498, fifth in Arkansas
Other townsMayflower, Vilonia, Greenbrier, Guy, Holland, Enola, Mount Vernon, Quitman, Wooster, Damascus
UniversityUniversity of Central Arkansas, founded 1907

What drives the Conway economy that sits behind Faulkner County values?

Conway's largest employers in May 2023 were Conway Regional Health System with 1,650 workers, the University of Central Arkansas with 1,600 and Acxiom with 1,450. Conway Public Schools, the Conway Human Development Center, Walmart, Gainwell Technologies, Virco and Home BancShares follow.

Conway had 64,134 people in 2020 and is home to three colleges: UCA, Hendrix College and Central Baptist College. Conway Public Schools reports about 10,000 students and 16 schools. Over 40 percent of Conway's adult workforce holds a bachelor's degree or higher.

Interstate 40 runs along the northern and eastern sides of Conway, and US 64 and US 65 also cross the city. Little Rock's Clinton National Airport is the main airport, and Conway has no passenger rail service today.

Outside Conway, Greenbrier and Vilonia are separate towns with their own schools and city rules. Check the school district and city on a tax bill before assuming the neighbor's bill applies to you.

Who handles property tax in Faulkner County?

The Assessor values property and the Collector bills and collects. Krissy Lewis is the Faulkner County Assessor, at 806 Faulkner Street in Conway, phone 501-450-4905, with a Greenbrier location at 89 N Broadview Street. Hours are 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday.

The Collector's page names Sherry Koonce, phone 501-450-4921. The Conway office is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. weekdays. The Greenbrier office, 89 N Broadview Street, runs Monday through Thursday 7:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. and Friday 8:00 a.m. to noon.

  • Mail, in-person and online payment are all accepted.
  • Online payments run through actdatascout.com/faulknerar, and a card fee applies.
  • Personal property tax must be paid with or before real estate tax, and the system will not take an electronic real estate payment until it is paid.
  • Statements go out in spring. The Collector says to call if yours has not arrived by July 1.

When are Faulkner County property taxes due?

Taxes are due from March 1 through October 15 and are collected one year in arrears, so 2020 taxes were due by October 15, 2021. A 10 percent penalty applies to real estate and personal property tax paid after October 15, and late real estate tax also accrues 10 percent annual interest.

Personal property must be assessed between the first working day of January and May 31. Missing that window brings a 10 percent late assessment fee, and a new purchase has 30 days to be assessed without penalty.

The state agency adds that if October 15 lands on a weekend or holiday, the next business day applies. In 2026, courthouse closures listed by the county include November 11, November 25 to 27, December 24 and 25, and December 31 through January 1.

How often does Faulkner County reappraise, and how do I appeal?

The Faulkner County Assessor says the current reappraisal cycle will be completed in 2028, and state pages describe reappraisal every 3, 4 or 5 years. An earlier public notice announced a three-year cycle from January 1, 2022, through December 31, 2024, with Total Assessment Solutions Corporation as contractor.

Because the two county pages do not describe the same schedule in the same words, ask the Assessor which year your neighborhood was last visited. The Assessor also notes that staff generally do not inspect interiors, and measurements come from the exterior and are approximate.

The County Board of Equalization exists to equalize assessed valuation under Arkansas Code 26-27-301 through 26-27-325. It has five members. Per the county's roster they are Steven Means, LuAnn Deere, Melinda Reynolds, Gelinda Mudgett and Eden Roberts, appointed by the Quorum Court, school districts, cities and towns and the County Judge. Members earn $100 per diem.

The state says the last day to schedule a hearing is the third Monday in August. Contact the Assessor first to see whether an error can be fixed informally.

What homestead credit applies in Faulkner County?

Faulkner County owners who live in the home can claim a homestead credit, and applications for the current tax bill are due October 15. The county's two pages disagree on the amount, with the Collector page saying up to $600 a year and the Assessor page saying up to $675.

A news report from April 2026 said the credit was $600 and that a $675 proposal had passed the Arkansas House 92 to 0 but still needed the Senate. Use the amount the Collector shows on your bill. Owners 65 or older or totally disabled may qualify for a freeze on taxable value of a principal residence. You must reapply when you move to a new home, so a buyer cannot simply inherit your credit.

What storm and flood history affects Faulkner County houses?

The April 27, 2014 tornado, rated EF4, killed 16 people across its 41.1 mile path and 12 of those deaths were in Faulkner County. It destroyed or heavily damaged homes in Mayflower and Vilonia, including the Parkwood Meadows subdivision in Vilonia and the River Plantation subdivision in Mayflower.

Homes along Lake Conway, described as the largest man-made Game and Fish Commission lake in the country, were also damaged. Conway itself had an F4 tornado on April 10, 1965. Conway's average annual precipitation is 51.19 inches.

  • Ask whether a roof, slab or storm shelter was rebuilt after a past storm.
  • Keep permit records for repairs.
  • Photograph damage you did not repair, since buyers will ask.

What does a sale and recording look like in Faulkner County?

The Circuit Clerk, Nancy Eastham, serves as ex-officio recorder at 724 Locust Avenue in Conway, phone 501-450-4911. Recording deeds costs $15 for the first page and $5 for each additional page, and plats and surveys are $15.

The clerk offers online land records and lists e-recording vendors, so a title company can file electronically. A free alert service emails you when a document is indexed under your name.

Arkansas also taxes the transfer at $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration, so a $200,000 sale is $660 according to the state Department of Finance and Administration. Records are also searchable at ARCountyData.com and ActDataScout.com, which the Assessor says update monthly.

More questions about Faulkner County, AR Property Tax Guide

Where do I pay Faulkner County property tax?

Pay the Faulkner County Collector at the courthouse in Conway, at the Greenbrier office, by mail or online. The Conway office is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday and the phone is 501-450-4921.

What is the penalty for paying Faulkner County taxes late?

Ten percent, applied after October 15. Real estate tax also accrues 10 percent annual interest.

Can I pay Faulkner County real estate tax online?

Yes, through actdatascout.com/faulknerar with a card fee. Personal property tax must be paid first, because real estate cannot be paid electronically until it is.

When will Faulkner County finish its current reappraisal?

The Assessor's page says 2028. State pages say counties reappraise every 3, 4 or 5 years.

How do I appeal a Faulkner County assessment?

Call the Assessor, then ask for a County Board of Equalization hearing. The state says the last day to schedule one is the third Monday in August.

Does a buyer keep my homestead credit?

No. Faulkner County says you must reapply when you move to a new location, and the owner who lives in the home claims the credit.

Garland County by the numbers

What makes Garland County different from other Arkansas counties?

Garland County is built around hot springs, lakes and the Ouachita Mountains, and Hot Springs is both the county seat and largest city. The county was formed on April 5, 1873, from parts of Hot Springs, Montgomery and Saline counties and is named for Governor Augustus H. Garland.

It covers 735 square miles, and 57 of those are water, about 7.7 percent. Lake Hamilton is the lake the county's own township and place names point to.

ItemDetail
FormedApril 5, 1873
County seatHot Springs
Area735 square miles, 57 of water
2020 Census population100,180
NeighborsPerry, Saline, Hot Spring, Montgomery, Yell
Named placesHot Springs Village, Lake Hamilton, Rockwell, Piney, Mountain Pine, Fountain Lake, Lonsdale

How does Hot Springs National Park shape land ownership here?

Hot Springs National Park is the state's only national park and is managed by the National Park Service, which puts a federal presence in the middle of the county seat. Congress set aside the Hot Springs Reservation in 1832 and the park was established in 1921, and the U.S. Supreme Court settled a property dispute in the federal government's favor in 1877.

Eight bathhouses stand on Bathhouse Row along Central Avenue, managed by the National Park Service. Buckstaff has operated continuously since 1912, and Fordyce Bathhouse became the park visitor center in 1989.

For a seller, the practical point is to confirm a parcel's boundaries and any federal or easement interests on a survey and title report, rather than relying on a neighbor's description.

What does the Hot Springs area economy look like?

Tourism anchors the economy, built on the thermal springs, Oaklawn Park and Magic Springs, with arts events such as the Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival. Oaklawn has run thoroughbred racing since 1904, with a December to May meet and the Arkansas Derby.

Hot Springs had 37,930 people in 2020, the 11th largest city in Arkansas, and the median age was 44.5. It sits about 55 miles southwest of Little Rock at an elevation of 568 feet.

  • US 70 and US 270 bypass downtown on the Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Expressway.
  • Arkansas Highway 7 runs through downtown, north to Russellville and south to Arkadelphia.
  • Arkansas Highway 128 reaches Red Oak, and Interstate 30 is about 17 miles away.
  • Hot Springs Intracity Transit runs three fixed bus routes, and Memorial Field is the local airport.

Five public school districts serve the city: Hot Springs, Lakeside, Cutter-Morning Star, Fountain Lake and Lake Hamilton. Which one a house falls in changes the millage on its bill.

Who bills and who values property in Garland County?

The Garland County Assessor values property and the Tax Collector bills it, and both offices are in the Government Office Building at 200 Woodbine Street in Hot Springs. The state lists Shannon Sharp as Assessor at Suite 123, phone 501-622-3730.

A 2020 local news article placed the Tax Collector at 200 Woodbine Street, Suite 108, with a 24-hour drop box behind the building. The county's online payment page lists 501-622-3710. Those details came from older pages, so call before a trip. The county homepage gives the courthouse at 501 Ouachita Avenue, phone 501-622-3600, and shows a tax and payment lookup on its quick links.

The county's courthouse and offices were listed as closed on November 26 and 27, 2026, for Thanksgiving.

When are Garland County taxes due?

Arkansas sets the payment deadline at October 15 for real estate taxes, and the Department of Finance and Administration says the next business day applies if that date falls on a weekend or holiday. Partial payments are generally accepted until then.

A Hot Springs newspaper story from a past year reported a 10 percent penalty for late payments, a 3.8 percent card convenience fee that the county did not keep, and a delinquent list sent for newspaper publication by December 1. Those were the figures for that year, and fees can change, so confirm with the collector.

Real estate is assessed to the owner of record as of January 1. If a house sells, the buyer's name goes on the tax roll based on the recorded deed, which is why a clean, timely recording matters.

How are Garland County values reappraised and challenged?

Reappraisal in Arkansas happens every 3, 4 or 5 years, and Garland County reported a five-year cycle in 2019 using a contracted appraisal firm. Assessed value is 20 percent of market value. We could not confirm the county's current cycle on an official page, so ask the Assessor for your parcel's last reappraisal year.

Amendment 79 froze assessed value for owner-occupied homes of seniors and disabled owners and capped yearly increases for owner-occupied homes at 5 percent. A home that rose more than 25 percent over a five-year cycle would not be taxed at its full new value when the next cycle ended.

The state says to check with the Assessor first, because errors in property details can be fixed informally. For a value dispute, the last day to schedule a County Board of Equalization hearing is the third Monday in August.

Can millage change for one town in Garland County?

Yes. In late 2019 the Garland County Quorum Court ratified millage rates that included a rollback for Mountain Pine's general fund, from 5 mills to 4.9 mills. State law requires a rollback when a tax base grows by more than 10 percent, and Mountain Pine's taxable assessed value rose 11.51 percent.

The growth came partly from close to $1 million in new construction, mostly a Morfe Windows plant finished in 2018 but not assessed until 2019. The small city's mills raised about $7,200 a year for its general fund. It was the only entity in the county with an adjusted rate that year.

The example shows why a new neighbor, a plant or a lake subdivision can alter a bill. Ask for the current millage for the exact school district and city when comparing parcels.

What should a Garland County seller do about taxes and recording?

Request a tax statement for the parcel, ask the title company to pay the balance from proceeds, and have the deed recorded promptly with the Garland County Circuit Clerk. Arkansas imposes a real property transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on deals above $100, which is $660 on a $200,000 sale, per the state Department of Finance and Administration.

For unpaid tax, the Commissioner of State Lands runs auctions of tax-delinquent land. Since Act 241 took effect on July 1, 2023, an auction sale is final, and owners can redeem until 4 p.m. on the last business day before the sale.

  • Order a survey if the house is near a lake or the national park boundary.
  • Confirm the school district and any improvement district on the bill.
  • Gather permits for work done on lakefront or older downtown homes.

Hot Springs also has a documented climate to consider: about 58 inches of rain a year, with May the wettest month, so check roofs, crawl spaces and drainage.

More questions about Garland County, AR Property Tax Guide

Where is the Garland County Assessor?

The Assessor is at 200 Woodbine, Suite 123, Hot Springs, AR 71901, and the phone number is 501-622-3730, per the state's county officials list.

When is the Garland County property tax deadline?

October 15, or the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday. Partial payments are generally accepted before then.

How do I appeal a Garland County assessment?

Contact the Assessor first, then request a County Board of Equalization hearing. The last day to schedule one is the third Monday in August.

Is land inside Hot Springs National Park taxable?

We could not confirm that on an official page. The park is federal land and was established in 1921, so check any parcel near its boundary with a title company.

What is the Arkansas transfer tax on a Garland County sale?

$3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transactions above $100. A $200,000 sale would carry $660.

Can a Garland County house with unpaid taxes still be sold?

Yes, if the balance is paid at closing before an auction. After a Commissioner of State Lands auction, the sale is final under Act 241.

Craighead County by the numbers

Where is Craighead County and what does it cover?

Craighead County sits in northeast Arkansas and has two county seats, Jonesboro in the western district and Lake City in the eastern district. The county was created on February 19, 1859, and covers about 713 square miles, with Crowley's Ridge running through it.

Jonesboro is the largest city. Other incorporated places include Lake City, Bono, Black Oak, Caraway, Brookland, Monette, Bay, Egypt, Cash and Nettleton, which sits partly inside Jonesboro. A property tax bill here therefore depends on which city, school district and improvement district the parcel falls in, not only on the county.

Total area713 square miles, about 707 of it land
County seatsJonesboro and Lake City
2020 Census population111,231
Neighboring Arkansas countiesGreene, Mississippi, Poinsett, Jackson, Lawrence
CollegesArkansas State University, ASU Newport Jonesboro Technical Campus

The county's western edge meets Jackson County, and to the northeast it touches Dunklin County, Missouri.

Who sends the tax bill and who sets the value?

In Craighead County two offices do separate jobs: the Assessor sets the value and the Tax Collector bills and collects the money. The county lists Hannah Towell as Assessor at 511 S. Union St., Suite 130, Jonesboro, telephone 870-933-4572, according to the state's county officials list.

The Tax Collector's Office, led by Wes Eddington, is at 511 Union Street, Suite 107, Jonesboro, with a second office at 107 Cobean in Lake City. The phone number is 870-933-4560.

The county explains that collections are turned over to the County Treasurer at the end of each month for distribution. Most of the money goes to schools. The rest is split among county offices, cities, fire and police pensions, libraries, roads, streets and improvement districts, depending on where the property sits.

  • Assessor: appraises property and takes personal property reports.
  • Tax Collector: mails bills, takes payment, publishes delinquent lists.
  • County Treasurer: receives and distributes the monthly collections.
  • Circuit Clerk: records deeds and mortgages.

How is Craighead County property tax calculated?

Taxable value is 20 percent of the Assessor's appraised value, and that figure is multiplied by the millage rate for the location. One mill equals one tenth of a cent, as the county's collector page describes it.

The county's own tax primer gives an example with a 42.20 millage rate on an assessed value of $2,015, which produces $85.03. The rate itself is voted on by taxpayers in the area, so two houses with the same value can carry different bills.

Real estate is assessed to the owner of record as of January 1. Taxes run one year behind, so the 2025 assessment is billed in 2026. If you sell during the year, the bill for the prior assessment year is still outstanding until paid, and it is usually settled through the title company at closing.

Arkansas appraisers also revisit properties on a schedule. The state's Assessment Coordination Division says reappraisal occurs every 3, 4 or 5 years, and that the appraiser looks at size, quality and condition of improvements, along with sales and rental data. Owners who add a room, build a garage or turn an owner-occupied house into a rental should tell the Assessor.

When are Craighead County taxes due and what happens if they are late?

The Tax Collector accepts payments from the first business day of March through October 15 of the year after the assessment. The county's page says the last day to pay 2025 taxes without penalty is October 15, 2026.

After that date the taxes are delinquent, a 10 percent penalty is added under Arkansas Code 26-35-501, and delinquent real estate taxes accrue interest daily. A payment sent by mail counts as timely if it is postmarked by October 15, and the collector suggests buying postage at the counter or asking for a hand postmark.

  • Online payment is offered through the county's payment portal.
  • For delinquent personal property, the office takes cash, money order, cashier's check or card (fees apply) and no personal checks.
  • The collector must publish delinquent lists each year. The personal property list goes to a local newspaper before December 1.

Personal property is separate from real estate, but unpaid personal property can complicate a payment day. Ask the office what is attached to your name before you plan a closing.

How do I appeal a Craighead County assessment?

Start with the Assessor, because wrong square footage or a wrong property description can often be corrected without a hearing. If the dispute is about value, the state says the last day to schedule a hearing with the County Board of Equalization is the third Monday in August.

The Assessor's office is the place to ask for the current equalization schedule and forms. The board hears the owner's side and decides whether to adjust the value.

Homeowners may also qualify for a credit. Arkansas pages describe a homestead credit under Amendment 79 for a principal residence, and a freeze on taxable value for owners 65 or older or totally disabled. The county's tax explainer lists a $375 credit, an older figure. A news report from April 2026 put the current credit at $600 and said the legislature was considering $675, so check the Assessor before counting on a number.

What is on the Craighead County ballot about the collector?

County voters were asked on November 3, 2026, whether to merge the elected treasurer and tax collector into one Collector/Treasurer office starting January 1, 2031. The Quorum Court voted 8 to 5 on February 9, 2026, to put the question on the ballot, according to the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension county fact sheet.

That fact sheet lists the 2026 county budget at $59.8 million and says the Tax Collector's office has nine employees. We did not confirm the election result on an official page, so the current structure stays in place for planning purposes. Any merger would not take effect until 2031.

What happens to a Craighead County property with unpaid taxes?

Unpaid taxes can lead to a tax-delinquent land sale run through the Arkansas Commissioner of State Lands. In August 2025, a regional auction covering Craighead, Mississippi and Poinsett counties was held at the Hilton Garden Inn Ballroom, 2840 S. Caraway Road, Jonesboro, according to a local news report.

Bidding starts at the taxes, penalties and interest owed. Owners can redeem until 4 p.m. on the last business day before the sale, and under Act 241, effective July 1, 2023, a sale at auction is final. Parcels that do not sell appear on an online list about 30 days later.

A sale before that point can stop the clock. A buyer who closes through a title company gets the bill paid from the proceeds, and nothing is left to certify.

What does selling a house in Craighead County involve?

A sale is recorded with the Circuit Clerk, who acts as county recorder. Craighead County's fee schedule lists $15 for the first page of a deed, $5 for each additional page and a $300 cap on multi-instrument documents.

Arkansas also charges a real property transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on deals above $100. On a $200,000 sale that is $660, per the Department of Finance and Administration. The state page does not say who pays, so that is settled in the contract.

  • Get a payoff or tax statement from the Tax Collector.
  • Check whether any personal property tax sits under the same owner name.
  • Confirm the deed's legal description against the Assessor's parcel record.
  • Ask the title company to pay the tax and record the deed the same day.

If the house has tenants, gather the lease and rent records before you list, since a buyer and the title company will ask for them.

More questions about Craighead County, AR Property Tax Guide

Who collects property tax in Craighead County?

The Craighead County Tax Collector, Wes Eddington, collects it at 511 Union Street, Suite 107 in Jonesboro and 107 Cobean in Lake City. The phone number is 870-933-4560.

What is the property tax deadline in Craighead County?

October 15 each year. The county's page says 2025 taxes were due without penalty by October 15, 2026, and later payments carry a 10 percent penalty plus daily interest on real estate.

How do I challenge my Craighead County assessment?

Contact the County Assessor first, then request a hearing before the County Board of Equalization. The state lists the third Monday in August as the last day to schedule one.

Does a mailed payment count if it is postmarked by October 15?

Yes. The collector cites Arkansas Code 26-35-501(c)(3)(A) and recommends getting a manual postmark at the counter to avoid delays.

Can I sell a Craighead County house that owes back taxes?

Yes. The tax is paid from sale proceeds at closing. A tax-delinquent parcel can still be sold at a state auction, which is final, so settle the balance before the sale date if you want to keep the property.

What does recording a deed cost in Craighead County?

The Circuit Clerk lists $15 for the first page and $5 for each extra page. Arkansas adds a transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration.

Benton County by the numbers

Where is Benton County, Arkansas, and how is it laid out?

Benton County is in the far northwest corner of Arkansas, on the Springfield Plateau of the Ozarks, bordering Missouri to the north and Oklahoma to the west. It covers about 884 square miles, and Beaver Lake, a White River reservoir along the eastern edge, holds most of the county's water.

The legislature created the county on September 30, 1836, from Washington County, and named it for Missouri senator Thomas Hart Benton. Bentonville became the county seat in 1837. Union troops burned the courthouse in 1862, and the present courthouse dates from 1928. Rogers is the largest city.

Other communities include Bella Vista, Bethel Heights, Cave Springs, Centerton, Decatur, Gentry, Gravette, Little Flock, Lowell, Pea Ridge, Siloam Springs and Sulphur Springs. Springdale and Elm Springs lie mostly in Washington County, though parts reach into Benton.

What does the Benton County economy depend on?

Walmart is the dominant influence. The company is headquartered in Bentonville and was founded in Rogers. Other large employers named in the county's history include Daisy Outdoor Products in Rogers, J.B. Hunt Transport Services in Lowell, Simmons Foods in Siloam Springs, and a Tyson Foods distribution center in Rogers.

Agriculture still shapes the land. Poultry, cattle and hog farming are the main rural uses, while tourism and construction round out the economy.

Population followed the jobs. The county had 153,406 residents in 2000, 221,339 in 2010 and 284,333 in 2020, the second largest in Arkansas. The 2025 estimate is 332,554. Median household income is the highest in the state.

Values rose 67.5 percent across the 2021 to 2024 reappraisal, which Assessor Rod Grieve said was slightly above what he expected. He pointed to an imbalance between housing supply and demand. The county crossed 300,000 residents in 2022.

The state's 2023 annual report listed Benton as a three-year cycle ending in 2024, done in-house. The assessor's FAQ now points to a county-wide reappraisal in 2028 and sends readers to a separate reappraisal website. Statewide, Arkansas assesses at 20 percent of appraised value, and Arkansas Business reported annual increases capped at 5 percent for a primary residence and 10 percent for commercial and industrial property.

The Baxter County assessor makes the same point about her own county: caps and freezes mean taxes do not rise at the pace of market value. A buyer comparing two houses should ask what each one's capped value is, not only its appraisal.

What do the assessor's rules mean for a seller and a buyer?

The assessor's FAQ spells out several rules that change how a sale plays out.

  • After a sale, the property is assessed at 20 percent of its appraised value at the next assessment date after title transfers.
  • A buyer who receives title by sale cannot claim an assessment limitation until the second assessment date after the transfer. Amendment 79 caps the assessment on a principal residence once the owner is 65 or older, and it does not cap taxes.
  • The homestead credit is described as up to $600, covers the full bill if taxes are lower, and applies to a primary residence only, one credit per calendar year. The Homestead Department is at 479-271-1037.
  • The freeze applies to taxable value, not to taxes, so a higher millage rate can still raise the bill. Owners 65 or older, or on Social Security Disability, qualify.
  • Adding on to a home removes the freeze and reapplies it at the new value.

The FAQ also notes that home-based businesses are taxable, and business personal property tax is due October 15, paid one year behind.

When and how do you pay Benton County property tax?

Taxes for 2025 were due by 11:59 p.m. on Thursday, October 15, and after that date a 10 percent late fee and or interest applies. The collector's calendar shows tax books opening the first business day of March, May 31 as the deadline to assess, and July 1 as the last day to mail statements.

  • Taxpayers with more than 50 parcels under one taxpayer ID cannot pay online, and payments post within 24 to 48 hours.
  • E-checks and phone payments have not been accepted since November 1, 2019.
  • A tax information request form for title companies is on the collector's site, which helps at closing.

Baxter County's collector also uses October 15, but each county posts its own details, so confirm the figures for the county where the house sits.

How did the 2024 tornado affect Benton County?

On May 26, 2024, an EF3 tornado 1.8 miles wide struck Benton County, described by Wikipedia as the largest tornado in Arkansas history. For anyone selling a house hit by that storm or a repaired one, a basic question for a buyer is whether the repair work was finished before listing.

Owners with storm-damaged houses sometimes choose to sell as-is instead of repairing, since a lender-backed buyer may require the work to be completed. A cash buyer can look at the house in its present condition.

What does the Benton County terrain mean for a house?

The county sits on karst, so springs, sinkholes and caves are part of the landscape. Wikipedia lists five watersheds, and notes that the highest point is Whitney Mountain near Lost Bridge Village.

Protected land breaks up the map. Pea Ridge National Military Park, Hobbs State Park-Conservation Area, Logan Cave National Wildlife Refuge, Devil's Eyebrow Natural Area and part of the Ozark National Forest all lie inside the county. Houses near that land and along Beaver Lake can have lot shapes, slopes and access roads that differ from a flat subdivision lot, so it is worth asking an inspector about drainage and the foundation on such a property.

What roads and airports serve Benton County sellers?

US 62 and US 71 run through the county, following the route once used by the Trail of Tears, and a railroad parallels both highways. Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) is near Highfill, and Rogers Municipal Airport (ROG) serves the county and nearby towns.

Most of the cities listed above sit along or near those corridors. Because a sale restarts the assessment clock for a new owner, a seller in Bentonville, Rogers or Bella Vista should know both the house's last appraised value and when the next county-wide reappraisal is due.

When is the Benton County property tax deadline?

October 15 at 11:59 p.m. for 2025 taxes. After that, the collector's page says a 10 percent late fee and or interest applies.

Who handles property tax appeals in Benton County?

The assessor sets value and the county equalization board hears appeals. Under section 26-27-317, an owner may apply to the board on or before the third Monday in August, and the board must give written notice of its decision after the hearing.

Does the homestead credit transfer to a buyer?

No. The credit is for a primary residence and one credit may be claimed per calendar year, and a buyer must apply on their own. A buyer who gets title by sale cannot claim an assessment limitation until the second assessment date after the transfer.

How can I get a tax figure for a closing?

Benton County posts a tax information request form for title companies on the collector's website, along with a tax record search where you can print receipts.

Is there a fee to pay Benton County taxes by card?

Yes. The county's online vendor charges $3.99 for payments of $110 or less and 3.59 percent above $110.

Pulaski County by the numbers

Where is Pulaski County and how is it laid out?

Pulaski County sits in central Arkansas, and its seat is Little Rock, which is also the state capital. Wikipedia gives the county 808 square miles in total, of which 760 are land and 48 are water.

The county touches six others: Faulkner to the north, Lonoke to the east, Jefferson to the southeast, Grant to the southwest, Saline to the west and Perry to the northwest. It forms the core of the Little Rock, North Little Rock and Conway metropolitan area, and its two townships are Big Rock and Hill.

Besides Little Rock, the cities and towns inside the county include North Little Rock, Jacksonville, Maumelle, Sherwood, Alexander, Cammack Village and Wrightsville. A seller in Pulaski County can be dealing with very different neighborhoods, school districts and city rules depending on which of these the house sits in, even though one assessor and one collector serve all of them.

The county was formed on December 15, 1818, as Arkansas's fifth county, and it was named for Casimir Pulaski, the Polish-born officer killed at the Siege of Savannah. Its 2020 census population was 399,125, the largest of any Arkansas county, and the 2025 estimate listed there is 404,611.

What drives the Pulaski County economy?

Health care, banking, transportation, manufacturing and state government carry most of the Pulaski County job base. The county seat hosts the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences, which Wikipedia's Little Rock entry puts at more than 10,552 employees, along with Arkansas Children's Hospital, the Central Arkansas Veterans Healthcare System and Baptist Health Medical Center.

Corporate names tied to Little Rock include Dillard's, Simmons Bank, Bank OZK and Stephens Inc., plus Entergy, Siemens and Dassault Falcon Jet. The Metro Little Rock Alliance adds FIS with about 1,300 professionals, Tyson Foods in North Little Rock, L'Oreal USA in North Little Rock, and Kimberly-Clark and Dillard's facilities in Maumelle.

Freight matters here too. The Port of Little Rock is an intermodal river port with a large industrial complex and is designated Foreign Trade Zone 14. Clinton National Airport is reached from Interstate 440, and the city lists Interstates 30, 40, 430, 440, 530 and 630 along with U.S. 65, 67, 70 and 167.

For a seller, this mix means a house near a hospital campus or a bank office tends to have a different buyer pool than one in a commuter pocket of Sherwood or Maumelle.

What does the climate mean for a Pulaski County house?

Pulaski County has a humid subtropical climate, so roofs, gutters and crawl spaces take hot, wet weather for much of the year. The Little Rock entry on Wikipedia lists about 50.4 inches of average annual precipitation, a record high of 114 degrees on August 3, 2011, and a record low of minus 12 degrees on February 12, 1899.

Winters are cool and usually bring little snow. The practical result is moisture. Moisture is the main wear factor on a roof, a crawl space or a bathroom floor, and a buyer who orders an inspection will look at each. A direct sale to a cash buyer skips the inspection negotiation, though the price still reflects the condition.

Which Pulaski County areas have a distinct character?

Little Rock's own neighborhoods include The Heights, Hillcrest and Pleasant Valley, and the Quapaw Quarter holds three National Register historic districts with at least a hundred listed buildings. Other listed districts are Capitol-Main, Central High School and MacArthur Park.

Jacksonville, on the northeast side, grew around military and industrial use. The city's land includes the former Arkansas Ordnance Plant, and some of that land was sold for development of Little Rock Air Force Base in 1955. Jacksonville's school district split from the Pulaski County Special School District after voters approved the separation on September 16, 2014, and the Jacksonville North Pulaski School District began on July 1, 2016. The Pulaski County Special School District continues to serve other parts of the county, so the district can change from one area to the next.

Who runs property tax in Pulaski County?

Three county offices touch a Pulaski County tax bill: the assessor values it, the clerk handles the appeals calendar, and the treasurer collects. The state's county officials list gives the assessor as Janet Troutman-Ward, at 201 S. Broadway, Suite 310, Little Rock, with phone 501-340-6170.

The County Clerk contact page lists the clerk at 401 W. Markham St., Suite 100, with a main line of 501-340-8500 and a Real Estate department at 501-340-8433. It names the County Treasurer as Debra Buckner, reachable at 501-340-8345 for payment questions.

How does the 2026 equalization calendar work for Pulaski County owners?

The Pulaski County Clerk's 2026 equalization timeline puts the last day to schedule a hearing at August 17, the third Monday in August. Assessment notices go out in July, and the clerk's office starts scheduling Equalization Board appointments on July 13.

  • August 3: the board holds its first meeting to organize and receives the real and personal assessment rolls from the assessor.
  • August 17: last day for an owner to schedule a hearing based on the assessment notice.
  • September 30: last day of the regular equalization meetings.
  • October 1: first day the board may meet in special session, if one is needed.
  • October 12: second Monday in October, the last day to take an appeal to County Court.

The timeline lists a second date for the County Court deadline, so confirm it with the clerk before relying on a single day. A special session, when the ratio of assessed value to market value falls short, may run into the third Monday in November.

Bring evidence. Recent sales of similar nearby houses, photographs of defects and any repair estimates are the usual materials, and the burden is on the owner to show the value is wrong.

What limits how fast a Pulaski County assessment can rise?

Arkansas caps the yearly increase in taxable value at 5 percent for a homestead and 10 percent for other real property. Under Amendment 79 as summarized by the state, those caps hold until the property reaches full assessed value, and they do not apply to new construction, newly discovered property or substantial improvements, meaning renovations that add 25 percent or more to value.

For an investor or landlord, the 10 percent cap on non-homestead property matters most. A rental that was far below market at the last reappraisal can climb by 10 percent a year until it catches up.

Homeowners also have the homestead credit, listed at up to $500 a year and up to $600 beginning with 2026 bills. Those who qualify and are 65 or older, or disabled, can have taxable value frozen. The state is clear that the freeze does not pass to a buyer. If you sell, the next owner starts fresh and may see a bigger bill than you did.

What happens to property tax when a Pulaski County house sells?

Arkansas collects property tax in the year after the assessment, so a Pulaski County closing often falls while a bill is still unpaid or not yet issued. Ask the closing agent how the bill is divided between seller and buyer and get that figure in writing.

The state also charges a transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of actual consideration on transactions over $100, under Ark. Code 26-60-101 and following, according to the Department of Finance and Administration. On a $200,000 sale that works out to $660, and the state sells the transfer stamps.

Back taxes are the common complication. If the property is behind, ask the Treasurer for the full payoff, including penalty and fees, so it can be settled from the sale proceeds.

What do Pulaski County sellers usually run into?

  • An inherited house with several years of unpaid tax and no one living there.
  • A rental with tenants in place and a reappraisal notice showing a higher value.
  • An older Little Rock or North Little Rock house with moisture damage that makes a retail listing difficult.
  • A house inside one of the Quapaw Quarter or other listed historic districts that a buyer may hesitate over.
  • An owner relocating for a job at a hospital, bank or the air base on short notice.

Any of these can be handled by a direct sale to a buyer who purchases as is, which removes repairs and showings from the timeline. Compare any written offer against the tax and lien payoff on your statement so you know the net figure.

Who do I call about my Pulaski County property assessment?

Call the Pulaski County Assessor at 501-340-6170 or visit 201 S. Broadway, Suite 310 in Little Rock. The assessor values property, while the County Clerk at 501-340-8500 schedules Equalization Board hearings.

What is the last day to appeal a Pulaski County assessment in 2026?

August 17, 2026 is the last day to schedule an Equalization Board hearing, according to the clerk's 2026 timeline. A further appeal to County Court is due by the second Monday in October, which is October 12 this year.

Is Pulaski County on a four year reappraisal cycle?

Yes. The state's 2025 report shows Pulaski County's four year cycle ending in 2026, with the work done in house across 177,110 parcels.

Does my senior tax freeze go to the buyer if I sell?

No. The state says the age 65 or disabled freeze does not transfer to a new owner, so a buyer's taxable value is set fresh at the next assessment.

How much is the Arkansas transfer tax on a Pulaski County sale?

It is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transactions over $100. On a $150,000 sale that is $495.

Can I sell a Pulaski County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes, the back taxes are normally settled from the sale proceeds. Ask the Treasurer at 501-340-8345 for a payoff figure before you sign anything.

Baxter County by the numbers

Where is Baxter County, Arkansas, and what towns does it include?

Baxter County sits in the Ozark Mountains of north-central Arkansas, on the Salem Plateau, just south of the Missouri line. It covers 586.74 square miles, and 5.5 percent of that is water, mostly Bull Shoals Lake and Norfork Lake, which give the area its Twin Lakes nickname.

The legislature created the county on March 24, 1873, from parts of Fulton, Izard, Marion and Searcy counties, and named it for Governor Elisha Baxter. It was Arkansas's 66th county. Mountain Home is the county seat and the largest city, with 12,825 residents in the 2020 census. The other incorporated places are Cotter, Gassville, Briarcliff, Norfork, Salesville, Lakeview and Big Flat, which lies partly in Searcy County.

Neighbors are Fulton County to the east, Izard to the southeast, Stone to the south, Searcy to the southwest, Marion to the west and Ozark County, Missouri, to the north.

What drives the Baxter County economy?

Lake tourism, health care and retirement spending carry most of the local economy. The Norfork and Bull Shoals dams, built in the 1940s and 1950s, brought construction jobs and then visitors, and a trout hatchery at the base of Norfork Dam opened in 1957. Bull Shoals Dam was dedicated on July 2, 1952, with President Truman speaking.

Baxter Regional Medical Center, founded in 1963, is one of the two institutions the Encyclopedia of Arkansas says dominate Mountain Home, with about 100 physicians and 1,000 employees. Arkansas State University-Mountain Home is the other. The county has three public school districts: Mountain Home, Cotter and Norfork.

The older population shapes the housing stock and the tax picture. The 2020 census put the median age at 52.7, and 31.5 percent of residents were 65 or older. That matters here because owners who are 65 or older, or disabled, can qualify for a freeze on their taxable value.

What are the key Baxter County numbers?

Who runs property tax in Baxter County?

Three offices split the work: the assessor values property, the County Clerk's office takes equalization board requests, and the collector bills and receives payment. The collector's office is at #8 East 7th Street, Mountain Home, AR 72653. The phone is 870-425-8300, and live support runs Monday through Friday, 8:00 to 4:30. The Baxter County Courthouse is at 1 East 7th Street.

The current assessor is Jayme Nicholson Johnson. The collector turns tax revenue over to the county treasurer at least monthly. Receipts have not been printed automatically since 2016, so mailed payments should include an email address or a self-addressed stamped envelope, and owners can sign up for e-statements and e-receipts.

What is the 2026 Baxter County reappraisal, and what happens in August?

Baxter County is one of five north-central counties reappraising in 2026, alongside Marion, Izard, Stone and Boone. A 2023 state law requires counties to appraise real estate at current market value at least every four years. The state's annual report lists Total Assessment Solutions Corp. as the Baxter contractor.

The last round raised values 35 percent across residential, commercial and new construction in 2022, according to the assessor. She stressed that is market value, not what owners paid, because caps and freezes keep taxes from rising at the same rate.

  • Anyone who bought a home in 2025 should expect a sales validation form to complete.
  • Notices go out in July to owners whose values increase.
  • Appeals are scheduled with the equalization board in August and heard in September.
  • The homestead credit was $500 in 2024 and $600 for 2025, and owners over 65 or fully disabled may qualify for a freeze on top of it.

Under section 26-27-317, an owner may apply to the equalization board on or before the third Monday in August. The board must give written notice of its decision at least ten business days after the hearing, and the notice must explain the right to appeal to county court.

When are Baxter County property taxes due?

Collection runs from the first business day of March through October 15. Taxes unpaid after October 15 are delinquent, and a 10 percent penalty applies to real or personal property tax not paid by then.

  • Installment payments are accepted between the first business day of March and October 15.
  • Before December 1, the collector sends the delinquent list to a legal newspaper, which must publish it within seven days.
  • Online payment runs through links to arkansastaxsearch.com.
  • Personal property such as vehicles and boats must be assessed by May 31 each year, according to University of Arkansas extension guidance.

Arkansas bills in arrears, so the bill that arrives in March reflects the prior assessment year. A seller who closes in the spring should ask the title company how the unbilled current-year tax is being handled.

What if tax stays unpaid on a Baxter County house?

Unpaid real estate tax can eventually lead to the land being certified to the Commissioner of State Lands, which sets up a sale. Under section 26-37-301, the Commissioner must notify the owner and recorded interest holders and offer redemption on payment of all taxes, penalties, interest and costs.

The sale date must be at least one year after certification. For a homestead, if there is no proof the owner received the certified mailing, the Commissioner must arrange personal service at least 60 days before the sale. Anyone with no ownership interest may also act as a redeemer by paying the amounts due.

For a seller, the practical point is timing. The collector can tell you what is owed, and asking for that payoff figure before you set a closing date avoids surprises.

What do sellers in Baxter County usually face?

A county with an older population and a lot of lake property raises a few situations again and again. Mountain Home's median age was 49.1 in 2020, and 32.1 percent of its residents were 65 or older.

  • Inherited houses where heirs live in other states and the property sits empty.
  • Homes with deferred maintenance, since a lender-financed buyer may require repairs.
  • Owners whose reappraisal notice raised the value and who want to sell before the new bill arrives.
  • Tax or insurance bills that have piled up during a long illness or move to care.

Weather and roads matter too. Mountain Home gets about 50.86 inches of precipitation a year and 7.8 inches of snow, with a record high of 114 degrees. There is no Interstate in the county. US 62 and US 412 run together east to west, and Arkansas 5 is the only route running north to south throughout. The nearest commercial airport is Springfield-Branson in Missouri, though the county has its own Baxter County Airport.

More questions about Baxter County, AR Property Tax Guide

When is the Baxter County property tax deadline?

October 15. The collector accepts payment from the first business day of March through that date, and unpaid tax is delinquent afterward with a 10 percent penalty.

How do I appeal my Baxter County value?

Request a hearing with the county equalization board through the County Clerk's office. Hearings can be scheduled starting in August, and state law sets the application deadline at the third Monday in August.

How much is the Arkansas homestead credit in Baxter County?

The local news report on the 2026 reappraisal says the credit was $500 in 2024 and $600 for 2025. Confirm the current amount with the assessor's office before you rely on it.

Can I sell a Baxter County house with unpaid property tax?

Nothing we read from the county bars a sale while tax is owed, but the amount due, including the 10 percent penalty after October 15, has to be settled. Ask the collector at 870-425-8300 for a payoff figure before you set a closing date.

Which Baxter County towns have their own school district?

The county has three public school districts: Mountain Home, Cotter and Norfork.

Where is Saline County and what does it include?

Saline County is a central Arkansas county southwest of Little Rock, with Benton as its seat and largest city. Wikipedia records its formation on November 2, 1835, and says the name comes from the area's salt water springs.

The county covers 730 square miles, of which 724 are land. It borders Perry to the northwest, Pulaski to the northeast, Grant to the southeast, Hot Spring to the southwest and Garland to the west, and part of the Ouachita National Forest lies inside it.

Places within the county include Benton, Bryant, Bauxite, Alexander, Avilla, East End, Haskell, Salem, Shannon Hills, Traskwood and part of Hot Springs Village. One assessor and one collector serve all of them, so a seller in any of these towns follows the same county calendar.

How fast is Saline County growing?

Saline County counted 123,416 people in the 2020 census, and the 2025 estimate on its Wikipedia page is 133,288. The median age in 2020 was 40.0, and density sits near 170 people per square mile.

That growth is the backdrop for the reappraisal notices covered below.

What shaped the Saline County economy?

Salt, pottery and bauxite made Saline County, and today it is mostly a commuter county tied to Little Rock. Benton's early industries included a salt works opened in 1827, pottery from local kaolin beginning around 1900, and logging and furniture making.

Bauxite, the ore for aluminum, left the deepest mark. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas says one of the state's two mining districts lies northeast and east of Benton, and that Reynolds Metals ran the company town of Bauxite from the early 1900s until 1969. Mining peaked during World War II, and Reynolds closed its Hurricane Creek plant in early 1982, the last year bauxite was mined in Arkansas for aluminum metal. Major reclamation programs to restore mined land began in the early 1990s.

Bryant also grew with that demand. Rail service in the 1870s brought development, the early 20th century and the Great Depression were hard years, and demand for bauxite revived the town around World War II.

Hot Springs Village crosses the Garland and Saline county line. The Saline portion is in the Little Rock metropolitan area, according to Wikipedia, and the community was founded June 1, 1970, with a private property owners' association that governs it. Its 2020 population was 15,861 and the median age 68.9.

Interstate 30 and Interstate 530 cross the county, along with U.S. 65, 67, 70 and 167 and Arkansas highways 5, 9 and 35. Wikipedia describes both Benton and Bryant as suburbs of Little Rock, and the interstate links are how the two cities connect to the capital.

Public schools come from several districts. Per Wikipedia's Benton page, the Benton School District serves most of the city, Bryant Public Schools runs Bryant High School, the Bauxite School District covers its own area, and the Harmony Grove School District serves a small area near Frontage Road.

Check the district for the exact address, because the same street can fall in different districts, and some buyers decide on the district first.

What does the climate mean for a Saline County house?

Benton has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and mostly mild to cool winters. Using 1991 to 2020 normals, Wikipedia lists 53.41 inches of precipitation a year and about 1.3 inches of snow, with a record high of 112 degrees and a record low of minus 17.

With that much rain, drainage, gutters and roof condition are reasonable things for a buyer's inspector to check.

The Saline County Collector's page names Jennifer Carter as collector, with phone 501-303-5620 and email info@salinecollector.org. It describes taxes as collected from March 1 through October 15 of the year after they are assessed, and lists in person, mail and online payment. In person, the office accepts cash, checks, cashier's checks, money orders, debit and major credit cards, and by mail personal checks are accepted only for current taxes.

The notices are not tax bills, and the higher values will not appear on the October 2026 payment. A KATV report dated July 21, 2026 quotes county communications director Trevor Villines saying Arkansas requires a countywide reappraisal every four years and that increased values take effect the following year.

Notices go only to owners whose value rose, so a property that fell in value gets no letter. The report says some residents were confused, some receiving a notice for the first time.

  • Call the Saline County Assessor's Office first if the value looks wrong.
  • If you still disagree, appeal to the Saline County Equalization Board.
  • Requests are filed with the county clerk, and the state deadline is the third Monday in August.

In 2017 the assessor's bid notice described a countywide reappraisal of about 74,732 parcels using software from Apprentice Information Systems, against the 78,135 in the state report now.

How do assessment caps and credits affect a Saline County sale?

A Saline County buyer's taxable value can step up by up to 5 percent a year on a homestead and 10 percent on other real property, until it reaches full assessed value. Arkansas's property tax relief page says new construction, newly discovered property and substantial improvements are outside the caps.

The homestead credit is up to $500 a year, rising to $600 for 2026 bills. A seller aged 65 or older, or disabled, who gets the credit can hold the assessed value steady, but the freeze does not move to the buyer. The buyer applies on their own after purchase.

What do Saline County sellers usually face?

  • Heirs of a Benton or Bryant house who live elsewhere and want to settle it before the next tax season.
  • Owners of rental houses with a reappraisal notice and a tenant on a lease.
  • Sellers at Hot Springs Village who must deal with the property owners' association along with county offices.
  • Houses with deferred roof or drainage repairs after wet seasons.

A direct purchase fits when repairs and showings are the obstacle. Compare any offer to your payoff and the collector's figure so you know what you would net.

No. The county says notices are sent only when a property's value rises.

Every four years. The state's 2025 report shows the current Saline County cycle ending in 2026, using Trimark Appraisals across 78,135 parcels.

Can I sell a Saline County house that has delinquent taxes?

Yes. Ask the Collector at 501-303-5620 for a payoff amount, and plan for the balance to be paid from the sale proceeds.

Where is Arkansas County, and why does it have two county seats?

Arkansas County sits in the Arkansas Delta in the eastern half of the state, almost entirely within the Grand Prairie subregion of the Mississippi Alluvial Plain. It is named for the Arkansas River, and it shares its name with the state rather than with a town.

Wikipedia lists the county at 1,033.79 square miles, of which 988.49 is land. It has two county seats: Stuttgart for the northern district and DeWitt for the southern district. DeWitt replaced Arkansas Post as the seat on February 19, 1853, and Stuttgart became a dual seat in the 1920s. The county was created from New Madrid County in 1813 and is the first of the state's 75 present counties.

For a property owner the two districts matter in a practical way. Both the assessor and the collector keep an office in each seat, so a seller in the north can handle paperwork in Stuttgart and a seller in the south can use DeWitt.

What is the land like, and what is the local economy?

The county is flat farmland laced with bayous and bounded by water. Its borders follow the Arkansas River, Bayou Meto and the White River, and La Grue Bayou runs through the interior.

Rice is the main crop, and the county lies in the largest rice-growing region in the United States. Soybeans, cotton, corn and wheat are also grown. Duck and goose hunting along the Mississippi Flyway draws visitors, and agricultural spraying dominates activity at the county's airports.

Stuttgart supplies most of the non-farm employers. Wikipedia names Riceland Foods, a farmer-owned rice cooperative headquartered there, along with Producers Rice Mill, a Lennox air conditioner factory, Stratton Seed, Layne Arkansas, Baptist Hospital, the University of Arkansas Dale Bumpers Rice Research Center and Delta Plastics. The World Championship Duck Calling Contest takes place in Stuttgart during Thanksgiving week.

  • Dale Bumpers White River National Wildlife Refuge covers 99.3 square miles along the eastern edge.
  • George H. Dunklin Jr. Bayou Meto Wildlife Management Area covers 39.3 square miles in the west.
  • Arkansas Post National Memorial and Arkansas Post State Park mark the old colonial trading post.
  • U.S. Highway 165 links DeWitt and Stuttgart with Little Rock, and Highway 130 runs between the two seats through Almyra.

How many people live here, and what do the housing numbers show?

The county had 17,149 residents in the 2020 census, down from 19,019 in 2010, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 15,836. Stuttgart fell from 9,326 to 8,264 over the same decade, and DeWitt from 3,292 to 3,056.

Who runs property tax in Arkansas County?

Two elected county offices split the work: the assessor values the property and the collector bills and receives the payment. The state's county directory on Arkansas.gov lists both, each with an office in DeWitt and one in Stuttgart.

Older directory pages, including some vendor sites, show different office-holder names and phone numbers, so confirm with the state's county page before you call or mail a payment.

When are Arkansas County property taxes due, and what is the penalty?

Under Ark. Code 26-36-201, real estate tax is payable to the collector from the first business day of March through October 15. If October 15 falls on a weekend or a postal holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day.

Taxes unpaid after October 15 are delinquent, and a 10% penalty applies. The state's own property tax pages say the same: the Department of Finance and Administration states that taxes are payable to the county collector by October 15 each year, and that partial payments are generally accepted up to the deadline.

  • First business day of March: collector can take payment.
  • Third Monday in August: last day to schedule a hearing with the county board of equalization, per DFA.
  • October 15: payment deadline, with the next business day applying if it lands on a weekend or holiday.
  • After October 15: delinquent, with a 10% penalty.

A sale does not reset any of this. The bill follows the parcel, so a seller who closes in September with the year's tax still open should ask the collector for the balance and settle it through the closing.

How do assessments and appeals work for an Arkansas County house?

The assessor values each property at market value and reappraises it every three, four or five years, according to DFA. The valuation uses a sales comparison, cost or income approach. An error in the property's description, such as the square footage, can often be corrected by calling the assessor before a formal appeal.

If the owner disagrees with the value, DFA says the last day to schedule a hearing with the county board of equalization is the third Monday in August. A board decision can be appealed to County Court and then to Circuit Court, as described on a neighboring county's assessor FAQ, which also explains statewide Amendment 79 limits.

Those limits are worth knowing before a sale. The same FAQ says reappraisal increases in taxable value on a primary residence are capped at 5% a year, that other real estate is capped at 10%, and that taxable value on the primary residence of an owner 65 or older, or disabled, cannot rise because of reappraisal. It also describes a homestead credit of up to $600, which the owner must claim with the assessor. A buyer's own tax bill may change when the new owner has to apply for these benefits.

What do sellers in Arkansas County usually run into?

Three situations come up more than any others in a county with this profile: inherited farm and town houses, rental houses with tenants, and properties with a tax bill that fell behind.

Inherited houses can move through the small estate procedure when the assets are modest. Ark. Code 28-41-101 sets a $100,000 ceiling, a 45-day wait and a published notice to creditors when real property is involved. Our statewide guide on Arkansas estate tax covers it in detail.

Tenant-occupied houses follow the state's landlord-tenant rules. The Attorney General says a landlord may end a lease for any reason with one rental period's notice for an oral lease, or as the written lease provides. Our guide on Arkansas eviction notices sets out the notice types.

Whatever the situation, closing triggers the state transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration, according to DFA, with the additional $2.20 per $1,000 described by statute as paid by the purchaser.

The county collector. The state's county directory lists Dean Mannis, 870-659-2104, with offices at 101 Court Square in DeWitt and 302 South College St. in Stuttgart.

When are Arkansas County property taxes due?

Real property tax can be paid from the first business day of March through October 15. Taxes unpaid after October 15 are delinquent and carry a 10% penalty under Ark. Code 26-36-201.

Where do I appeal my Arkansas County assessment?

Start with the assessor, who can correct simple errors. For a value dispute, DFA says the last day to schedule a county board of equalization hearing is the third Monday in August.

Which city is the county seat of Arkansas County?

There are two. Stuttgart serves the northern district and DeWitt serves the southern district.

What is the median home value in Arkansas County?

The Census Bureau reports a median value of owner-occupied housing units of $138,100 for 2020 to 2024. It describes the county as a whole, not any one house.

Can I sell my house if property taxes are still owed?

Yes. The tax follows the parcel, so ask the collector for the balance due and arrange for it to be paid from the sale proceeds at closing.

Sebastian County by the numbers

Why does Sebastian County have two county seats?

Sebastian County has two seats, Fort Smith and Greenwood, because of a long 19th century dispute that was settled in the 1874 state constitution. Wikipedia says the General Assembly created the county on January 6, 1851 as Arkansas's 56th, and an 1860 compromise divided it into two judicial districts named for their seats.

The seat moved back and forth during Reconstruction until the Arkansas Supreme Court ruled in 1872 that Greenwood was the lone seat while allowing courts in both cities. The 1874 constitution then said Sebastian County may have two districts and two county seats.

That is why county offices, including the assessor's real estate line, are listed for both Fort Smith and Greenwood.

Where is Sebastian County and how big is it?

Sebastian County is a western Arkansas border county of 546 square miles, the second smallest in the state by area. It includes 532 square miles of land and 14 of water, and it sits where the Arkansas River meets the Poteau River.

Neighbors are Crawford to the north, Franklin to the east, Logan to the southeast and Scott to the south, with Le Flore and Sequoyah counties in Oklahoma to the southwest and northwest. Parts of the Fort Smith National Historic Site and the Ouachita National Forest lie inside the county.

Communities named on the county page include Fort Smith, Greenwood, Barling, Bonanza, Central City, Hackett, Hartford, Huntington, Lavaca, Mansfield and Midland. The 2020 census counted 127,799 residents, the fourth most of any Arkansas county, with a 2025 estimate of 130,641, a median age of 38.2 and about 240 people per square mile. About 80.3 percent of residents live in urban areas.

What is the history behind Fort Smith real estate?

Fort Smith began in 1817 as a U.S. Army post at Belle Point on the Arkansas River, named for General Thomas Adams Smith. Wikipedia's Fort Smith entry says it later supplied the Mexican-American War, outfitted Gold Rush travelers and became a division center for the Butterfield Overland Mail in 1858.

Judge Isaac C. Parker presided from 1875 to 1896. The Fort Smith National Historic Site preserves the 1817 fort remains, his restored courtroom and a frontier jail nicknamed Hell on the Border. The Belle Grove Historic District is a 22 block downtown area with nearly 25 restored homes spanning 130 years of styles.

The Army established Fort Chaffee east of the city in 1941. It trained armored divisions in World War II and in 1975 served as a resettlement center for Vietnamese refugees.

How large is Fort Smith compared with the rest of the county?

Fort Smith is by far the largest city in Sebastian County, with 89,142 residents in the 2020 census and a 2025 estimate of 90,855, which makes it the third most populous city in Arkansas. Against the county's 127,799 residents in 2020, that is about 70 percent.

The county page also notes that a second fort built in 1836 marked the western end of the Trail of Tears, and that Cherokee settled the area after the 1811 and 1812 New Madrid earthquakes. Union troops captured Fort Smith on September 1, 1863 and withdrew in 1871.

Who are the largest employers in Fort Smith?

Mercy-Fort Smith leads the list with 3,413 employees, followed by Fort Smith Public Schools with 2,424, based on the city's 2024 annual financial report as quoted by Wikipedia. The ten largest employers there are shown below.

What does the weather mean for a Sebastian County house?

Fort Smith has a humid subtropical climate and sits near Tornado Alley, so storm wind is a fair concern for roofs. January averages 40.4 degrees and July 83.1, and records run from minus 15 on February 12, 1899 to 115 on August 3, 2011.

Wikipedia lists three major tornadoes for the city, in 1898, 1927 and April 21, 1996. The 1996 storm killed four people and damaged much of downtown.

A roof that has aged through years of storms can complicate a retail sale, because a buyer's inspector will check it. A buyer paying cash can take the roof as is.

Which roads link Sebastian County?

Fort Smith is served by Interstates 40, 49 and 540 and by U.S. 64, 71 and 271. The city sits just southwest of the I-40 and I-49 interchange, and I-49 is planned to extend south to Texarkana, Texas.

How does Sebastian County reappraise and notify owners?

Sebastian County's reappraisal cycle ended in 2025 and runs five years, with Total Assessment Solutions Corp as the contractor. The state's 2025 assessment report lists 56,876 parcels, about $2.36 billion in 2024 taxable value (summed from its categories) and a total millage of 52.38.

The county assessor's value guide explains the steps. Appraisers visit to measure buildings and record condition, the county reviews sales from the final reappraisal year, keeps typical market sales, and uses them to value similar homes nearby. Values are set as of January 1.

  • Previous Value: the current full appraised value.
  • New Value: the full value on current market conditions.
  • Taxable Value: the figure used for next year's taxes, after caps and freezes.
  • Estimated Tax Change: the difference at the current millage rate.

Owners are mailed a notice only if the value went up. The guide also says the county caps increases at 5 percent for an owner occupied homestead and 10 percent for other property, with no new construction.

The assessor, Zach Johnson, is listed by the state at 35 S. 6th, Room 104 in Fort Smith, phone 479-784-1516.

How should you prepare an appeal in Sebastian County?

Start with the informal review and gather sales of comparable nearby houses, because the owner carries the burden of proof. The county's appeal page suggests checking the assessor's data for errors such as wrong square footage and asking for the comparable sales the assessor used.

It also notes that appraisers typically see only the exterior, so a cracked foundation or pest damage that you can document may support a lower value. The Board of Equalization has nine members drawn from school districts, cities and towns, the County Judge and the Quorum Court.

What else does the Sebastian County assessor say about taxes at sale?

The county's FAQ says city liens must be paid before or with taxes, so a lien on the property can surface at closing. It also says homestead credit applications for the previous year are due October 15, and that owners 65 or older, or disabled, can freeze value with proof of age or disability.

The state says that freeze ends with your ownership, so a buyer starts from the current value.

Personal and business property can be assessed from January 1 through May 31 without penalty, and after that the state adds a 10 percent penalty that cannot be removed.

Why does Sebastian County have two county seats?

An 1860 compromise created two judicial districts, and the 1874 Arkansas Constitution confirmed that Sebastian County may have two districts and two seats, Fort Smith and Greenwood.

When did Sebastian County last reappraise?

The state's 2025 report lists the cycle ending in 2025, a five year cycle handled by Total Assessment Solutions Corp across 56,876 parcels.

Do Sebastian County owners get a notice if their value drops?

No. The assessor mails a notice only when a property's value increases.

How much can my Sebastian County assessment rise in a year?

By up to 5 percent for an owner occupied homestead and up to 10 percent for other property, as long as there is no new construction.

Who do I call to start an informal review?

Call the reappraisal firm at 479-424-2624. For the petition and hearings, call the County Clerk at 479-782-5065.

Can a buyer keep my senior tax freeze?

No. The state says the freeze does not transfer when the property is sold.
